title: Working out resources & availability
blurb: Turn the WBS and estimates into a resource requirement, check it against real availability, and spot over-allocation on a histogram.
question: Northgate Council is replacing its payroll system. The plan needs the payroll team to test the new system in March, the same month they run year-end. How should the project manager determine what resources are required, and why must availability be checked separately?

teach.h: Two questions: what do we need, and what can we get?
teach.body: APM describes resource management as the ability to identify and schedule the internal and external resources a project requires. In practice that means two separate jobs. First, work out the REQUIREMENT: for each activity, what type of resource, which skills, how much and when. Second, check AVAILABILITY: what is actually free in those periods once leave, other projects and business-as-usual work are taken out. The plan is only realistic where the two match.

teach.note: A named person on the team list is not the same as a person available every day.

teach.caption: A histogram plots demand for one resource per period. Bars above the available level show over-allocation that must be resolved before the plan is baselined.

teach.body: Checking requirement against availability early (capacity planning) gives a schedule people can actually deliver. It exposes clashes while there is still time to re-sequence, negotiate with line managers, book suppliers or recruit. It also makes cost estimates honest. Skip it and the plan quietly over-allocates people: fatigue, mistakes, missed dates and damaged relationships with the BAU managers whose staff you borrowed.

teach.h: Linear and iterative: the same idea, different grain
teach.body: In a LINEAR life cycle the PM builds the requirement bottom-up for every activity, loads it against availability for the whole project, then refines it at each phase. In an ITERATIVE life cycle the team is usually fixed for each time box, so the question flips: what is this team's capacity, and is the product owner and any specialist available for every iteration? Scope is then chosen to fit.

teach.text: Exam trap: an option that describes a REQUIREMENT (effort, skills, quantity) when the question asks about AVAILABILITY (leave, BAU, other projects, lead times), or the reverse. Also watch for 'resources' meaning only people: equipment, facilities, materials and money are resources too.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Start from the WBS and estimates: list each activity's resource type, skills, quantity and timing.
Check availability: calendars, leave, other projects, BAU commitments and supplier lead times.
Compare demand with supply using a resource histogram to find over-allocation or gaps.
Resolve gaps: re-schedule, smooth or level, negotiate, or bring in external resource.
Explain the benefit: a realistic, agreed plan with fewer delays and honest costs.
Requirement comes from the work: WBS and estimates give type, skills, quantity and timing.
Availability is separate: leave, BAU, other projects, part-time allocation and lead times.
A resource histogram shows demand per period against what is available.
Resources include people, equipment, facilities, materials and money.
Iterative teams start from a fixed team's capacity and fit scope to it.

summary: You can now build a resource requirement from the WBS and estimates, covering type, skills, quantity and timing, and test it against real availability. You can read a resource histogram, spot over-allocation and explain why resolving it early makes the plan deliverable.

A.q: When determining the resources a project needs, what should the project manager start from?
options: The staff currently free to help
A.why: Requirements come from the work: each work package and activity in the WBS, with its estimate, tells you the type, skills, quantity and timing needed.

whyNot.0: Who is free is availability. Starting there shapes the plan around people rather than around the work.
whyNot.1: Preferences may matter later, but they do not tell you what the work actually requires.
whyNot.2: Historic headcount says nothing about what this project's activities need.

A.q: Which of the following is NOT a factor in assessing resource availability?
options: Leave already booked by team members
Commitments to other projects and BAU
Effort each activity needs to finish
A.why: The effort an activity needs is part of the REQUIREMENT (demand). Availability is about what supply is actually free.

whyNot.0: Booked leave directly reduces how much of a person is available.
whyNot.1: Other projects and BAU work compete for the same people, so they reduce availability.
whyNot.3: Lead times decide when external equipment or contractors can actually be available.

A.q: What does a resource histogram show a project manager?
options: Demand for a resource in each period
Who is accountable for each package
A.why: A resource histogram plots how much of a resource is needed in each time period, usually against the level available, so peaks of over-allocation stand out.

whyNot.1: Sequence and dependencies are shown on a network diagram or Gantt chart.
whyNot.2: Accountability is shown on a responsibility assignment matrix (RACI).
whyNot.3: Cumulative spend is shown on a cost S-curve, not a resource histogram.

B.q: Northgate Council's payroll officers are needed to test a new system in March, the month they run year-end. What is the best description of the planning problem?
options: The WBS has missed a work package
The supplier should do the testing
The histogram is using the wrong scale
B.why: The requirement is valid, but year-end is a business-as-usual peak that reduces how much of the payroll team is actually available in March.

whyNot.0: Testing is in the plan; the problem is when the people can do it, not missing work.
whyNot.1: Users need to test their own system; handing it to the supplier removes user acceptance.
whyNot.2: The issue is real availability, not how the chart is drawn.

B.q: A business analyst is allocated to a project for 2.5 days a week and spends the rest on BAU work. How should the resource plan treat her?
options: As fully available to the project
B.why: Her availability to the project is half of each week, so the plan should load no more than 2.5 days of project work per week on her.

whyNot.0: Assuming full availability would over-allocate her by double.
whyNot.2: She is available, just partly; ignoring her wastes real capacity.
whyNot.3: People are re-usable resources; replenishable resources such as materials are used up.

B.q: A draft plan books a tester at 150% of his available hours for six weeks. What is the most likely result if this is not resolved?
options: Lower costs from the extra productivity
B.why: Over-allocation is not sustainable: quality drops, work runs late and the dates that depend on it slip.

whyNot.0: Overloaded people are less productive per hour, and overtime usually adds cost.
whyNot.1: Over-allocation tends to lengthen delivery, not shorten the critical path.
whyNot.3: Dependencies come from the logic of the work, not from how loaded a person is.

C.q: A construction project needs a specialist crane that can only be hired with 12 weeks' notice. Why must this be captured when determining resources?
options: Cranes must be bought rather than hired
So it is booked in time for the schedule
So the crane appears on the OBS chart
Lead times only matter in iterative work
C.why: Supplier lead time is part of availability. Capturing it early means the crane is ordered in time to be on site when the activity is scheduled.

whyNot.0: Hiring is a perfectly normal way to source equipment; buy or hire is a separate decision.
whyNot.2: The OBS shows the people and organisations doing the work, not equipment bookings.
whyNot.3: Lead times affect any life cycle; linear construction projects depend on them heavily.

C.q:
Which TWO of the following describe resource REQUIREMENTS rather than availability?
1) Three electricians needed in weeks 4–6
2) An electrician on leave in week 5
3) 40 m² of flooring for the ground floor
4) The training room booked by HR in May
C.why: Items 1 and 3 state what the work needs (type, quantity and timing). Items 2 and 4 describe constraints on supply, which is availability.

whyNot.0: Item 2 (leave) is an availability constraint, not a requirement.
whyNot.2: Both 2 and 4 are availability constraints: leave and a room already booked.
whyNot.3: Item 4 is about the room's availability, not what the work needs.

C.q: The histogram shows demand for data analysts above availability in weeks 6–7. What should the project manager do first?
options: Tell the team to work overtime then
Remove the weeks 6–7 work from scope
Accept the overload as normal in practice
Look at re-scheduling or extra resource
C.why: The first step is to explore options: re-schedule within float, smooth or level, negotiate more analyst time or bring in external help, escalating if none works.

whyNot.0: Planned overtime hides the problem and risks fatigue and errors; it is not a first response.
whyNot.1: Cutting scope needs change control and sponsor agreement; it is a last resort, not a first step.
whyNot.2: Accepting over-allocation leads to slippage and poor quality.

reteach.title: Planning a family wedding
reteach.question: You are organising a wedding for 120 guests in June. How do you work out what you need, and why is it not enough to know which suppliers exist?

blocks.h: Need first, then who is free
blocks.body: Start from the jobs: a venue for 120, a caterer, a photographer, 40 chairs, flowers and a budget. That is the REQUIREMENT: type, quantity and timing (the second Saturday in June). Then check AVAILABILITY: the photographer you love is booked that day, the venue's calendar has one Saturday free, and the florist needs eight weeks' notice. Your plan only works where need and availability meet.

blocks.caption: Just like a resource histogram: two peaks above what is available, spotted early enough to ask the venue for staff or set up the night before.

blocks.text: Knowing a resource EXISTS (there are photographers in town) is not the same as knowing it is AVAILABLE when you need it (free on your date, with enough notice).

explain.body: The WBS breaks the scope into work packages and activities. Each one, with its estimate, tells you what it needs. Building the requirement this way makes sure no work is left unresourced and nothing is resourced that is not in scope.

test.q: Which document is the best starting point for listing the resources each activity needs?
test.why: The WBS (with estimates) defines every piece of work, so it is the basis for working out what each piece needs.

whyNot.1: The stakeholder register records who has an interest, not what work needs resourcing.
whyNot.2: The issue log tracks problems that have arisen, not the planned work.
whyNot.3: Lessons learned can improve estimates, but they do not define this project's work.

explain.body: A complete requirement states the type of resource (person, equipment, facility, material, money), the skills or specification, how much (person-days, units) and when in the schedule. 'Some IT people' is not a requirement; 'two SQL data analysts, 30 days, weeks 4–8' is.

test.q: A plan says 'two qualified electricians, 15 person-days, weeks 3–5'. Which aspects of the requirement does it capture?
test.why: 'Qualified electricians' is the skill, '15 person-days' the quantity and 'weeks 3–5' the timing.

whyNot.0: No cost, risk or quality information is given.
whyNot.2: It does not say who owns or approves the work.
whyNot.3: No supplier, contract or price is mentioned.

explain.body: Ask line managers and suppliers what is genuinely free in each period. Take off leave, training, other projects, BAU peaks and any part-time split, and allow for supplier lead times. Get the commitment agreed, not assumed.

test.q: Which is the best example of checking resource availability?
options: Estimating how long each activity will take
Asking line managers when staff are free
test.why: Availability is confirmed with the people who control supply, such as line managers, taking account of leave and other commitments.

whyNot.0: Estimating effort is part of the requirement, not availability.
whyNot.1: Decomposing deliverables builds the WBS, the source of requirements.
whyNot.3: Sequencing builds the schedule logic; it does not check who is free.

explain.body: Plot demand for each key resource per period on a histogram against what is available (capacity planning). Peaks above the line are over-allocation. Resolve them before baselining: re-schedule within float, smooth or level, negotiate more time, bring in contractors, or escalate.

test.q: On a resource histogram, demand in week 10 rises above the available level. What does this indicate?
options: The activity is on the critical path
The package has no accountable owner
The budget is overspent that week
test.why: Demand above availability in a period means more of the resource is needed than exists: over-allocation.

whyNot.1: Criticality comes from the network and float, not from resource demand.
whyNot.2: Ownership is shown on a RACI, not a histogram.
whyNot.3: A resource histogram shows quantity of resource, not spend against budget.
